sentences.text: Approximately 1,200 specimens of Pteranodon are known to science, more than any other pterosaur, many featuring well-preserved skulls and articulated skeletons.
Othniel Charles Marsh described Pteranodon as distinguished from all previously known pterosaur genera by the complete absence of teeth.
Unlike earlier pterosaurs, Pteranodon possessed toothless beaks similar to those of birds.
The neural spines of Pteranodon's vertebrae were narrow.
In 1876, Marsh recognized Pteranodon as a unique genus because it completely lacked teeth, a trait not seen in other pterosaurs at that time.
Fossil specimens show that females and juveniles had small crests while males had large, elaborate, and variable crests.
The average wingspan of an adult male Pteranodon was 5.6 meters.
Adult females were much smaller, averaging a wingspan of 3.8 meters.
The largest known Pteranodon longiceps from the Niobrara Formation had a wingspan of 6.25 meters.
A larger specimen with a 7.25-meter wingspan is known from the Pierre Shale Formation.
Pteranodon was the first pterosaur species discovered outside of Europe.
The first Pteranodon skull was discovered on May 2, 1876, by Samuel Wendell Williston along the Smoky Hill River in Kansas.
S. W. Williston was the first scientist to critically evaluate all Pteranodon species previously classified by Cope and Marsh.
Pteranodon likely took off from the ground using a standing, quadrupedal position.
Pteranodon used its long forelimbs to vault itself into the air during takeoff.
Trackway evidence suggests that Pteranodon moved on land as a quadruped.
Fossilized fish bones found in the stomach area and a fish bolus found between the jaws of specimen AMNH 5098 confirm that fish were part of Pteranodon's diet.
A 1993 study found subadult Pteranodon had fibrolamellar bone, indicating rapid growth.
Methods for estimating the mass of large male Pteranodon with wingspans around 7 meters have been notoriously unreliable.
A 2010 review by Witton and Habib argued that the maximum mass of Pteranodon is likely between 20 and 35 kg, rather than 93 kg.
The wing shape of Pteranodon suggests it may have flown similarly to a modern albatross.
In 1904, Barnum Brown reported that the stomach area of a plesiosaur contained bones of a pterodactyl, very likely Pteranodon.
It is known that at least some of these marine reptiles fed on Pteranodon.
Pteranodon belongs to the family Pteranodontidae and the clade Pteranodontia, which also includes nyctosaurids.
In 1972, Halsey Wilkinson Miller proposed that different forms of Pteranodon should be classified into distinct subgenera.
Many species of Pteranodon named since the 1870s are now considered junior synonyms of just two or three valid species.
Pteranodon lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically from the Santonian to Campanian stages.
Pteranodon inhabited North America during the Late Cretaceous, with fossils found in present-day Kansas, Nebraska, Wyoming, South Dakota, and Alabama.
Pteranodon fossils are found in the Smoky Hill Chalk of the Niobrara Formation and the Sharon Springs deposits of the Pierre Shale Formation.
Pteranodon was a significant component of the animal community in the Western Interior Seaway.
Pteranodon was an important part of the fauna in the Niobrara Sea.
The existence of P. maiseyi is uncertain, and some researchers debate whether P. sternbergi and P. maiseyi should be classified as the separate genus Geosternbergia.
The function of Pteranodon's skull crest remains a subject of scientific debate.
